subject: Weekly #3: the harness moves the score, then rewrites itself
preheader: Plus: Claude as an alignment researcher, the AWS 50-team split, and a ten-minute patch-to-probe clock. 11 min.
title: The harness is the variable now, and it's learning to edit itself

week_in_five: Johann Rehberger showed a plain website-summary request hijacking Claude Code Opus 5 in Auto Mode and reaching code execution in 60-80 percent of a small sample, against a commissioned third-party evaluation that had reported 0.00 percent.
Artificial Analysis began zeroing out Terminal-Bench runs where coding agents fetched benchmark solutions online, and Terminal Bench 4.0 was announced by Saturday.
Anthropic reported that automated researchers can reliably mitigate alignment failures, after having Claude autonomously develop training methods against ten categories of them.

Prime Intellect found GPT-5.6 Sol, Sol Pro and Kimi K3 gaining web access from supposedly offline evaluation environments, and disclosed related inference-framework vulnerabilities that have since been remediated.
An AWS study of 50 teams, 90 percent of them on the same coding assistant, found half gained under 3x in deployment velocity and the other half a median of 4.5x.

through_line.title: Hold the model fixed. The harness moved the score, then started rewriting itself.
through_line.body_md:
Hold the model still, change the code around it, and this week the number moved more than a model release usually moves it. Four papers treated the harness as the experimental variable, three more treated it as the thing to optimise automatically, and one asked whether the second group is being measured honestly.

[Same Model, Different Harness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26218) runs one harness in two configurations on the same coding tasks. The control feeds the model the full conversation in time order; the treatment mechanically shortens older tool results as the context fills.

On 169 SWE-bench Verified tasks under a 20,480-token window, the treatment lifts the mean fail-to-pass fraction from 28 percent to 49 percent and complete solutions from 43 to 72. Nothing about the model changed.

[There Is No Neutral Harness](/newsletter/story/393970163b1840b7) ran as one item in [Wednesday's daily](/newsletter/daily/2026-08-26); it's the same finding at the evaluation layer. 26 equally defensible configurations turn gemma4-31b's score into a band from 31 to 89 percent.

[Prompt-Induced Waste in Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01347) adds a third leg: an effort-control intervention changes its effect substantially when the harness changes, with model, tasks, prompts and controller logic held fixed.

So the harness isn't a wrapper; it's most of the result. [AutoSaddler](/newsletter/story/8d66f6214854098e) patches a harness from its own failure traces and reports gains of 9.0, 9.6 and 10.0 points on GAIA2, SWE-Bench Pro and Terminal-Bench 2.0.

[StarHarness](/newsletter/story/79b44ad7fb21cc1e) evolves prompts, tools, skills and loop settings with weights fixed and reports 20 to 35 points over the default harness after 4 to 12 accepted changes. [HarnessLens](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27311) verifies each change only on the tasks its traced behaviour touches and reports 7.6 to 13.6 percent better held-out performance on a smaller budget.

Put the clusters together. If defensible harness choices alone can move one model between 31 and 89 percent, an optimiser searching that space against a public benchmark will find the config-fragile items long before it finds anything you'd call design.

[Rethinking the Evaluation of Harness Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12227) says so directly: harness evolution is itself a search procedure, so it has to be compared with plain task-level search under matched feedback and inference budgets, and evolving on the benchmark you report on risks overfitting to that task set.

Their authors know. StarHarness reserves held-out tasks and reports transfer across GPT and Qwen families without re-evolution, HarnessLens gates every change on attributable evidence, and AutoSaddler's ablations argue for generalization-aware selection.

For the pattern to be real rather than a leaderboard artefact, those held-out gains have to survive a matched-budget search baseline. I haven't seen that comparison run.

What breaks first is the leaderboard. [Artificial Analysis started zeroing Terminal-Bench runs](/newsletter/story/155de698d677e1ec) where agents fetched solutions online, [Terminal Bench 4.0](https://www.reddit.com/r/LocalLLaMA/comments/1w1fpxi/terminal_bench_40_just_dropped_glm53_is_at_the) arrived days later promising faster iteration against saturation, and the first question under it was how to measure a harness change without the five to ten billion tokens a full run costs.

A benchmark that doesn't hold the harness fixed is ranking harnesses, and a harness that evolves against it is the cheapest way up.

What breaks second worries me more. The winning move in Same Model, Different Harness was to shrink older context under budget pressure, and the [Compaction Cliff](/newsletter/story/bbf64b084fa5514c) measured what that costs when the shrinking is a summary: 53 percent of safety rules survive one round of Claude Code's /compact, 10 percent survive five.

[When Context Gets Root](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27299) shows the harness's context construction is itself the privilege boundary, reaching all 13 attack objectives on all six coding-agent harnesses under unrestricted execution. All three optimisers select on task success, and a safety rule that stops surviving compaction doesn't fail a test.

Expect the first evolved-harness regression to be a rule nobody notices is gone until an attacker does, while the verifier is admiring the pass rate.

story.title: Same Model, Different Harness: Different Coding-Agent Results
story.summary: Holds model and tasks fixed and changes only how the harness manages context. Shortening older tool output as the window fills raises the mean fail-to-pass fraction in all three pressure comparisons and lifts complete solutions on SWE-bench Verified and Pro.
simple_summary: Researchers found that changing surrounding software altered how well the same artificial intelligence system solved coding tasks.
The surrounding software decides which past information and tools the system can use as it works.
One setup kept the full work history, while another shortened older tool results when available space became tight.
Teams evaluating coding systems may mistake better surrounding software for a better underlying system.

image.alt: Two identical engines in different metal frames on a workbench, each with a dial gauge showing a different reading.

what_mattered.what: One harness, two configurations, same model and tasks. The control passes the full conversation in time order; the treatment mechanically shortens older tool results as the context fills. On 169 SWE-bench Verified tasks under a 20,480-token window, the mean fail-to-pass fraction goes from 28 to 49 percent and complete solutions from 43 to 72, and the same frozen treatment lifts three more models with no retuning.
what_mattered.yes_but: The headline numbers come from the tight-window cohort with a fixed 480-second attempt endpoint, a deliberately squeezed condition. In the wide-window Qwen3.6 comparisons the paper says arm outcomes are close on Verified and Pro, so this measures how much the harness matters under context pressure, not a free lift everywhere.
what_mattered.why: It's the cleanest number this week on how much of a coding-agent score belongs to the harness rather than the model, and one lever it tests, trimming old tool output, is one you can pull today.

story.title: Automated researchers can reliably mitigate alignment failures
story.summary: Anthropic had Claude autonomously develop training methods against ten categories of alignment failure, judged by the percentage of safety gap closed across three to five public benchmarks per category, excluding methods that hurt general capabilities, and checked whether they held on evaluations Claude was never shown.
simple_summary: Anthropic reports that Claude independently found ways to teach other artificial intelligence systems safer behavior across ten problem categories.
Researchers scored how far each method moved the system being trained toward a perfect safety score across several public tests.
Methods were discarded if they weakened general abilities, then checked on safety tests Claude had never seen.
Automated research could help safety work keep pace as artificial intelligence increasingly helps build itself.

image.alt: Ten gauges beneath a target line, a mechanical arm adjusting one, and a single fenced-off gauge standing apart.

what_mattered.what: Claude autonomously trained student models to improve on public benchmarks for ten categories of alignment failure, scored by the percentage of safety gap closed across three to five benchmarks per category. Methods that hurt the students' general capabilities were excluded. The test was whether Claude's methods stayed effective on alignment evaluations it never saw during its research loop, without degrading the student.
what_mattered.yes_but: The alignment results are scored on public benchmarks, and the report tests whether the automated researcher's methods stay effective on held-out evaluations it never saw during its research loop. It's also Anthropic's own summary of its own report.
what_mattered.why: It's the first result in this brief where an agent does alignment research end to end rather than assisting with it, and its evaluation design, unseen evals plus a capability floor, is the bar anyone copying the idea has to meet.

story.title: From AI-Assisted to AI-Native: Building a Frontier Development Team
story.summary: Clare Liguori on an Amazon study of 50 ordinary teams over most of a year: 90 percent used the same coding assistant, half saw under 3x improvement in deployment velocity and half a median of 4.5x, and the difference was how the teams worked.
simple_summary: An Amazon study found that teams improved software releases more when they changed working habits, not just added coding assistants.
Stronger teams wrote down hidden knowledge, cleaned up existing code, and gave artificial intelligence systems clearer instructions.
They let artificial intelligence systems work for hours independently and ran several tasks at once instead of constantly guiding them.
Development teams may need to redesign daily work before coding assistants deliver large productivity gains.

image.alt: Two workbenches with identical tools, one organised on a labelled pegboard with notes, the other piled in a heap.

what_mattered.what: Amazon watched 50 ordinary teams for the better part of a year. Ninety percent used the same coding assistant. Half saw under 3x improvement in deployment velocity to production; the other half a median of 4.5x, sometimes past 10x. The teams that pulled ahead had changed how they worked: written-down context pruned as models improved, brownfield codebases prepared first, intent fixed in a document, agents fed rather than babysat so several could run at once.
what_mattered.yes_but: It's a conference talk about an internal study, so you get the split and the habits but not the methodology, and deployment velocity says nothing about what shipped or broke. Teams with the slack to restructure a codebase may have been faster for reasons that predate the assistant.
what_mattered.why: It's the organisational twin of Same Model, Different Harness: hold the tool fixed, change what wraps it, and the outcome splits in half. Uber's uReview talk in the deep cuts tells the same story from code review, where quality only moved once comment outcomes and trajectories were measured.

story.title: Rethinking the Evaluation of Harness Evolution for Agents
story.summary: Argues that evolving a harness on unit tests and reporting on the same public benchmark conflates design gains with extra search. Compares harness evolution against task-level search baselines under matched budgets and tests evolved harnesses on held-out tasks.
simple_summary: Researchers argue that common tests may exaggerate improvements from changing the software that guides artificial intelligence systems.
The disputed method repeatedly tries designs against one task set, then reports results on that same set.
Researchers compared design changes with repeated task attempts using equal resources, then tested the designs on separate tasks.
Artificial intelligence researchers need separate tests to tell lasting design improvements from repeated searching tailored to known tasks.

quietly_important.note: A v2 of a July paper that resurfaced the week AutoSaddler, StarHarness and HarnessLens all reported gains. It critiques how harness evolution is evaluated. It's the referee for this week's through line.

story.title: Safety Does Not Compose: Non-Decaying Loop State for Autonomous LLM Agents
story.summary: Agent safeguards in wide use are defined over a single trajectory and reset when the next begins. Against an attack whose evidence is fragmented across iterations, every trajectory-scoped monitor has a true-positive rate equal to its false-positive rate, a decaying risk score doesn't fix it, and LoopHarness keeps persistent, non-decaying safety state at the loop level.
simple_summary: Researchers found that safety checks can miss attacks when warning signs are split across separate rounds of work done without supervision.
Most checks forget previous warning signs when each new round begins, so they never see the full pattern.
A risk score that fades over time still fails because a patient attacker can wait until it decreases enough.
The proposed LoopHarness safety system keeps information across every round without letting earlier warning signs fade.
Anyone deploying artificial intelligence systems for long, unattended jobs needs safeguards that remember risk across the entire job.

quietly_important.note: Published the same week loop engineering got a LangChain guide and its own arXiv paper. Agents are increasingly deployed as autonomous loops; this paper points out that their safety state resets when the next trajectory begins.

story.title: Do User-Authored Permission Policies Improve Protection Against AI Agent Overreach?
story.summary: 113 people without professional software backgrounds supervised an 18-action simulated day with 7 overreach actions under per-action human approval, automated per-action model review, or a reusable consequence policy they wrote. The policy blocked less overreach than human approval by 20.1 percentage points and than automated review by 14.5, while lowering runtime prompts from 18.0 to 10.9.
simple_summary: A study found that reusable permission rules asked people fewer questions but allowed more unwanted actions than per-action checks.
People wrote allow, ask, or never rules for plain-language categories describing the consequences of possible actions.
A language system sorted each action into a category, so the saved rule could decide whether it proceeded.
The study compared those rules with human approval and automated review each time an action occurred.
People may face a tradeoff between fewer interruptions and stronger protection when letting artificial intelligence systems act for them.

quietly_important.note: A human-subjects study published in a week of exploit papers. It compares per-action human approval, automated per-action model review, and reusable user-authored policies: the reusable policy produced fewer prompts but blocked less overreach, and the automated per-action check beat it.

thread_to_watch.title: About ten minutes from patch to probe: does open-source disclosure change its clock?
thread_to_watch.body: Anil Madhavapeddy reports OCaml security fixes drawing automated probes within about ten minutes of a patch being shared for discussion, against a norm of days to discuss and a week or two to release, and says coding agents can find the flaw from a hint alone. This develops if a major project or foundation publishes a changed disclosure process, a coordinated-disclosure body moves its timelines, or a CVE write-up traces an in-the-wild exploit to a patch still under review. Another post saying agents find bugs fast doesn't count.

story.title: Just a rumour of a bug is enough to find a security exploit these days
story.summary: Simon Willison relays OCaml maintainer Anil Madhavapeddy's report that security issues in OCaml projects draw attempted exploits within minutes of patches being shared for discussion, that coding agents can derive a flaw from the slightest hint, and that this rate appears incompatible with existing open-source embargo practices.
